mainTopic: A field sold by someone who did not own it: when the buyer can back out, whether he recovers the שבח, and רבא's challenge to שמואל from the משנה about collecting שבח and produce
overview: The עמוד opens by finishing a ruling about a buyer of a contested field. Before he takes חזקה (by walking its borders) he may back out, but after that he may not. A second version says this holds even if the sale came with אחריות. Next, רב and שמואל argue about a field that turns out not to belong to the seller: רב says the buyer gets back his מעות and the שבח, while שמואל says only the מעות. רב הונא is unsure whether an explicit promise of שבח would help in שמואל's view, but רב נחמן reports that שמואל denies the שבח even then, because it looks like ריבית. רבא challenges this from a משנה in גיטין that lets שבח be collected from free property. The גמרא defends שמואל by reading that clause as a creditor case, and works through two ברייתות about שבח and produce. רבא explains the produce ברייתא as a robber who ate the produce and ruined the field. רבה בר רב הונא then begins another explanation, which continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: After taking possession, the buyer cannot back out
steps.stepSummary: This finishes a ruling begun just before. Before taking חזקה, the buyer of a contested field sold without אחריות may back out. Once he has taken חזקה, he may not, because he knowingly bought a 'tied-up sack.'
steps.simpleTranslation: He can back out. Once he took possession of it, he cannot back out, because the seller says to him: 'You knowingly accepted a tied-up sack.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a ruling about a buyer whose newly bought field is being challenged. Before taking חזקה he may cancel; after taking חזקה he may not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sale had no אחריות, so the buyer knew he was taking a risk, like buying a closed sack without seeing inside. Once he has formally taken the field through חזקה, the seller can tell him he accepted that risk, so the deal stands.

keyTerms.meaning: To back out of the deal
Took possession (made a חזקה)
A tied-up sack, whose contents you cannot see
You understood and accepted

phrases.english: he can back out of it.
phrases.notes: This finishes a sentence from just before: until the buyer takes possession, he may back out.

phrases.aramaic: מִשֶּׁהֶחְזִיק בָּהּ – אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לַחֲזוֹר בּוֹ.
phrases.english: Once he took possession of it, he cannot back out of it.
Because the seller can say to him:
You knowingly accepted a tied-up sack.
phrases.notes: Picture buying a sealed bag without knowing what's inside. That's what a sale with no guarantee is like.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשֶּׁהֶחְזִיק בָּהּ – אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לַחֲזוֹר בּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a ruling that began just before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Before חזקה the buyer may cancel. After חזקה he may not, since he accepted the risk of a sale without אחריות.

steps.title: When does taking possession happen?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks at what point the buyer counts as having taken חזקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: From when is it considered possession?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question. Since the rule turns on חזקה, it needs to know exactly when חזקה happens.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole ruling in step 1 hangs on the moment of חזקה. Before it the buyer can cancel, and after it he cannot. So the גמרא needs a clear definition of that moment.

keyTerms.meaning: From when?
Taking possession

phrases.english: From when is it considered possession?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a definition of the key term used in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact moment when the buyer's חזקה takes effect.

steps.title: Possession begins when he walks the borders
steps.stepSummary: חזקה happens once the buyer walks along the borders of the field.
steps.simpleTranslation: From when he walks along the borders.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the buyer counts as having taken חזקה once he walks along the field's boundaries.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Walking the borders shows he is treating the field as his own. From that moment he can no longer cancel the deal.

keyTerms.meaning: Treads, walks over
Borders, boundaries of a field

phrases.english: From when he walks along the borders.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: חזקה takes effect once the buyer walks along the field's borders.

steps.title: Another version: even with a guarantee he cannot back out
steps.stepSummary: Some say the buyer cannot cancel after חזקה even if the sale came with אחריות. The seller can say: show me a court document that the field is really being taken from you, and then I will pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: And some say: even with a guarantee too, because the seller says to him: 'Show me your court document of seizure, and I will pay you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of the ruling that extends it to a sale made with אחריות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, a guarantee does not let the buyer cancel just because people are challenging the field. The seller only has to pay once a court actually takes the field and gives the buyer a טירפא document. Until then, the sale stands.

keyTerms.meaning: A guarantee by the seller to pay back if the field is taken
Your court document of seizure
And I will pay you

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new opinion about a different case. It is another version of the same ruling, which applies it even to a sale with אחריות.

phrases.english: And there are those who say:
Even with a guarantee too, he cannot back out,
because the seller says to him: Show me your seizure document,
and I will pay you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a broader version of the ruling in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even with אחריות, the buyer cannot cancel after חזקה. The seller pays only once the field is actually seized by court order.

steps.title: רב and שמואל on repaying the improvement
steps.stepSummary: If someone sold a field that turned out not to be his, רב says the buyer gets back his מעות and the שבח. שמואל says he gets back his מעות but not the שבח.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: One who sells a field to another, and it turns out it was not his. רב said: He gets the money and he gets the improvement. שמואל said: He gets the money, but he does not get the improvement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a מחלוקת between רב and שמואל about what the seller must pay back when the real owner takes the field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both agree the buyer gets his purchase price back. They argue only about the added value the field gained while the buyer had it, the שבח.

keyTerms.meaning: Money, the price paid
Improvement, the added value of the field

steps.whatToRemember: רב says the buyer gets the price plus the שבח. שמואל says he gets only the price.

phrases.english: It was stated: One who sells a field to his fellow
and it turns out that it is not his,
Rav said: He (the buyer) gets the money
and he gets the improvement.
And Shmuel said: The money he gets,
the improvement he does not get.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר: הַמּוֹכֵר שָׂדֶה לַחֲבֵירוֹ וְנִמְצֵאת שֶׁאֵינָהּ שֶׁלּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a related but new question: what a seller of a field that isn't his must pay back.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: the buyer recovers the price and the שבח. שמואל: he recovers the price only.

steps.title: What if the seller explicitly promised the improvement?
steps.stepSummary: Students ask רב הונא whether שמואל would agree the buyer gets the שבח if the seller spelled it out. It depends on שמואל's reason. Was it only that the seller never promised it? Or was it that paying it looks like ריבית?
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked רב הונא: If he spelled out the improvement for him, what is the law? Is שמואל's reason that he didn't spell out the improvement, and here he did? Or perhaps שמואל's reason is that since the seller has no land, it looks like interest?
steps.whatsHappening: The students ask רב הונא a question that tests the reason behind שמואל's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If שמואל's only reason is that the seller never promised the שבח, then an explicit promise would work. But if his reason is that the field was never the seller's, then the price was really like a loan, and getting back extra money would look like ריבית. In that case even an explicit promise would not help.

keyTerms.meaning: They asked him
Spelled out, stated explicitly
Or perhaps
Looks like interest

steps.whyThisMatters: This question shows how a ruling's reason decides its limits. One reason allows a promise to help, and the other does not.

phrases.english: They asked Rav Huna:
If he spelled out the improvement for him, what is the law?

phrases.aramaic: טַעְמָא דִשְׁמוּאֵל מִשּׁוּם דְּלָא פָּירֵשׁ שְׁבָחָא,
phrases.english: Is Shmuel's reason because he did not spell out the improvement,
and here he did spell it out for him?
Or perhaps Shmuel's reason is:
since he has no land,
phrases.notes: The field was never the seller's, so the buyer's money was really just sitting with him, like a loan.

phrases.english: it looks like interest.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעוֹ מִינֵּיהּ מֵרַב הוּנָא: פֵּירֵשׁ לוֹ אֶת הַשֶּׁבַח מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Probes the reason behind שמואל's view in step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether an explicit promise of the שבח obligates the seller in שמואל's view. That depends on whether his reason is the missing promise or the look of ריבית.

steps.title: רב הונא answers 'yes and no' and stays unsure
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא answers 'yes and no,' and the matter stays unclear to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Yes and no, and it was unclear to him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא gives an uncertain answer, so he gives no firm ruling. The next step brings one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His 'yes and no' shows he could not decide between the two possible reasons for שמואל's view. רב הונא himself gives no ruling on whether an explicit promise of the שבח works. The next step settles it.

keyTerms.meaning: Yes and no
It was weak (unclear) in his hands

steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא could not decide whether an explicit promise of שבח helps in שמואל's view. The next step brings רב נחמן's report of שמואל, which settles it.

phrases.english: He said to them: Yes and no,
and it was unclear to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ: אִין וְלָאו, וְרַפְיָא בִּידֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the question of step 6 without resolving it.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No firm answer. רב הונא was unsure.

steps.title: שמואל: No improvement money even if it was spelled out
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן quotes שמואל: the buyer of a field that was not the seller's gets his מעות back, but not the שבח, even if the seller spelled out the שבח.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: רב נחמן said in the name of שמואל: the buyer gets back his money, but not the improvement, even if the seller spelled out that he would pay for the improvement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a clear ruling from שמואל that settles the question רב הונא could not answer in Step 7.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 6 asked whether שמואל would give the buyer the שבח if the seller spelled it out. This report says no: even an explicit promise does not help. This hints that שמואל's reason is not just that the seller never promised it.

keyTerms.meaning: Money. Here, the price the buyer paid.
Improvement. The added value the buyer gave the field.
He spelled it out, meaning he promised it clearly.

phrases.aramaic: אִיתְּמַר, אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: It was stated: Rav Nachman said in the name of Shmuel:
He has the right to the money,
phrases.notes: "He" is the buyer who bought a field that was not the seller's, the case from Step 5.

phrases.english: but he does not have the right to the improvement,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁפֵּירַשׁ לוֹ אֶת הַשֶּׁבַח.
phrases.english: even if the seller spelled out the improvement for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר, אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the question that stayed open for רב הונא in Step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Buyer of a field that was not the seller's gets his מעות back but never the שבח, even if the seller explicitly promised it.

steps.title: The reason: it looks like interest
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains שמואל's reason: since the sale never really took effect, the buyer's money was like a loan, so extra payment looks like ריבית.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? Since the buyer has no land, he would be standing and taking a fee for the use of his money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why a written promise does not help, and answers that collecting the שבח looks like ריבית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seller never owned the field, so there was no real sale. That makes the buyer's money look like a loan to the seller. Getting back the money plus the שבח looks like getting the loan back with extra, which is ריבית, and a promise cannot make ריבית allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?
Land.
A fee for the use of his money.
Interest, which the Torah forbids on loans between Jews.

steps.whatToRemember: According to שמואל, the buyer of a stolen field never gets the שבח, even with a written promise, because it looks like ריבית.
steps.confusionAlert: The buyer is not being punished here. The problem is that the extra money looks like ריבית on a loan.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
Since he has no land,
phrases.notes: The field was never the seller's, so the buyer never really got any land.

phrases.english: he would be standing and taking a fee for his money.
phrases.notes: Meaning it looks like ריבית on a loan.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא? כֵּיוָן דְּקַרְקַע אֵין לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for the ruling in Step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: שמואל's reason is that paying the שבח looks like ריבית, so even an explicit promise does not help. This is the second option raised in Step 6.

steps.title: רבא quotes a משנה about collecting improvement
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges רב נחמן with a משנה: certain payments, including שבח קרקעות, are not collected from sold property, because of תיקון העולם.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא raised an objection against רב נחמן: We do not collect from sold property for eaten produce, for the improvement of land, or for the support of a wife and daughters, because of the betterment of the world.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא quotes a משנה to set up a challenge. The next step will draw the point out of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists debts that cannot be collected from property the debtor already sold to others. One item on the list is שבח קרקעות, the improvement of land. רבא will use this mention of שבח against שמואל's ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: Property that was tied to a debt and later sold to someone else.
Betterment of the world. A rule made by חכמים to keep society working well.
Support of a widow and daughters, promised in the כתובה.

phrases.english: Rava raised an objection to Rav Nachman:
We do not collect for eaten produce,
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in גיטין 48b.

phrases.english: or for the improvement of land,
or for the support of the wife and the daughters
from sold property,
because of the betterment of the world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a משנה to challenge the ruling of Steps 8-9.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's report of שמואל that a buyer never collects שבח.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה lists שבח קרקעות as something that can be collected, just not from sold property. The full inference comes in Step 11.

steps.title: So improvement is collected from free property, even for a stolen field
steps.stepSummary: רבא infers that שבח is collected from the seller's unsold property, and argues that the משנה is talking about someone who bought from a thief.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is only from sold property that we do not collect. But from free, unsold property we do collect. And the משנה mentions improvement of land. Isn't that about someone who bought a field from a robber?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא draws the point from the משנה. A buyer of a stolen field does collect שבח from the seller's free property, which goes against שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the משנה only blocks collecting from sold property, it must allow collecting from unsold property. רבא assumes the שבח case is a buyer who bought a stolen field. That is exactly the case where שמואל said no שבח at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Free property that the owner still holds and has not sold.
It teaches. The source says this.
Is it not? It brings in the reading the challenger wants to prove.
One who buys from a robber.

phrases.english: It is from sold property that we do not collect,
but from free property, we do collect,
phrases.notes: Both words mean free, unsold property. Some versions leave out the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording.

phrases.english: and in any case it teaches about improvement of land,
isn't it about one who buys from a robber?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רבא's challenge by drawing the point out of the משנה quoted in Step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that a buyer of a stolen field gets no שבח.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה shows that שבח is collected from free property. If the משנה is about a stolen field, then paying שבח is not treated as ריבית, which goes against שמואל.

steps.title: No, the משנה is about a creditor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה is not about a stolen field. It is about a field taken from the buyer by the seller's בעל חוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is talking about a creditor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבא's reading. The משנה's case is a field taken away by a creditor, not a stolen field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the creditor case, the seller really owned the field, so the sale was real. The buyer's money was never a loan, so paying him the שבח does not look like ריבית. שמואל's ruling about a stolen field stays in place.

keyTerms.meaning: Creditor. Someone the seller owed money to before he sold the field.
No. It rejects the reading just offered.

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's שבח payment is about a field taken by a creditor. There the sale was real, so it is not ריבית. שמואל's rule for a stolen field still stands.
steps.confusionAlert: In both cases the buyer loses the field. The difference is whether the seller ever really owned it. In the creditor case he did, so there is no ריבית problem.

phrases.english: No, it is about a creditor.
phrases.notes: The seller owed money, and his creditor took the field from the buyer to collect the debt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's challenge by changing which case the משנה is talking about.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Case reassignment: the source is moved to a different case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא thought the משנה's שבח case was a buyer from a robber, which would go against שמואל.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about a field taken by the seller's creditor. The sale was real, so paying שבח is not ריבית, and שמואל's ruling stands.

steps.title: The produce clause cannot be about a creditor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the creditor reading. The first clause of the משנה, about produce, does not fit a בעל חוב, because שמואל says a creditor collects שבח but not produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the משנה is about a creditor, look at the first clause: 'One does not collect from sold property for produce that was eaten.' But does a creditor even get produce? שמואל said a creditor collects the improvement. So improvement, yes, but produce, no!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from Step 12 by looking at the first clause of the same משנה. That clause talks about produce, and a בעל חוב never takes produce.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first clause assumes the buyer lost the field's produce to whoever took the field. According to שמואל, a creditor takes the field and its שבח, but not the produce. So a creditor case would never involve lost produce, and the first clause must be talking about someone else.

keyTerms.meaning: A creditor, someone the seller owed money to
The first clause of a משנה or ברייתא
Produce of the field that was eaten or enjoyed
Improvement or increase in the field's value

phrases.english: If it is about a creditor,
say the first clause:
One does not collect from sold property for eaten produce,
and if it is about a creditor,

phrases.aramaic: בַּעַל חוֹב מִי אִית לֵיהּ פֵּירֵי?
phrases.english: does a creditor have any claim to produce?
But didn't שמואל say:
A creditor collects the improvement.
Improvement, yes,
but produce, no!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges Step 12's reading of the משנה as a creditor case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the משנה is about a field taken by the seller's בעל חוב.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first clause speaks of produce. Per שמואל, a creditor takes שבח but not produce, so the first clause cannot be a creditor case.

steps.title: So the whole משנה must be about a robber
steps.stepSummary: The first clause must be about a robber and his victim. Since the first clause is a robbery case, the last clause about שבח should be a robbery case too, and רבא's challenge comes back.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is obvious that the first clause is about a robber and the person he robbed. And since the first clause is about a robber and his victim, the last clause is also about a robber and his victim.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its push. If the produce clause is about robbery, the שבח clause in the same משנה should be about robbery as well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A robbery victim gets back his field together with its produce, so the produce clause fits a robbery case. The גמרא assumes both clauses of one משנה share the same setting. If so, the שבח clause is about a robber again, and רבא's challenge to שמואל from Step 11 returns.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious
A robber and the person he robbed
The last clause of a משנה or ברייתא

phrases.english: Rather, it is obvious it is about a robber and the one he robbed.
And since the first clause is about a robber and his victim,
the last clause is also about a robber and his victim.
phrases.notes: The 'last clause' is the part about שבח קרקעות, the rule רבא quoted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes Step 13's challenge by drawing the conclusion for the שבח clause.
steps.raayaObject: That the שבח clause of the משנה is about a robber, which brings back רבא's challenge.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The produce clause of the same משנה, which can only be a robbery case.

steps.title: Each clause can describe a different case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the idea that both clauses must share one setting. The produce clause is about a robber, and the שבח clause is about a creditor.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that a real comparison?! This clause is as it is, and that clause is as it is.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the idea that the two clauses must be about the same kind of case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing forces one משנה to keep the same setting in every clause. The produce clause can be about a robber while the שבח clause is about a creditor. That keeps the answer from Step 12 alive.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that a real comparison? Used to reject a link between two cases
This one is as it is, and that one is as it is. Each case stands on its own

phrases.english: Is that a real comparison?!
This one is as it is,
phrases.notes: The produce clause stays a robbery case.

phrases.english: and that one is as it is.
phrases.notes: The שבח clause stays a creditor case.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 14 by denying the assumption that both clauses share the same setting.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the inference from the first clause to the last clause. The point that the produce clause is about robbery is accepted.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It wrongly assumes that every clause of a משנה must deal with the same kind of case.

steps.title: A ברייתא sets the שבח case with a robber
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the split reading with a ברייתא. It explains the שבח rule with a robbed field: the principal is collected from sold property and the שבח from free property.
steps.simpleTranslation: But isn't it taught this way? How does the rule about improvement of land work? Someone robbed a field from another person, and the field is taken out of his hands. When he collects, he collects the principal from sold property, and he collects the improvement from free property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that explains the משנה's שבח rule, and it describes a robber, not a creditor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא explains the שבח clause with a stolen field, not a creditor. That seems to cancel the answer that the שבח clause is about a creditor. The next step works out who is collecting, and shows it must be a buyer from the robber, which is hard for שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: The principal, the value of the field itself
Property that is tied to a debt and has since been sold to others
Free property still owned by the debtor

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא places the שבח rule in a robbery case, which seems to undo the creditor answer. Step 18 shows how שמואל can still read it as a creditor case.
steps.whyThisMatters: Moving the שבח clause to a creditor case was how the גמרא defended שמואל. This ברייתא seems to block that route. Step 18 answers by reopening it.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught this way:
How does the rule about improvement of land work?
Someone robbed a field from his fellow
and it is taken out of his hands,
phrases.notes: As written, it sounds like the field is taken from the robber himself. The next step asks how that can work.

phrases.english: when he collects,
he collects the principal from sold property,
and the improvement he collects from free property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges Step 15's split reading with an explicit ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the שבח clause is about a creditor while the produce clause is about a robber.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא explaining the שבח clause describes a robbed field, with שבח collected from free property. Step 17 shows that this must mean a buyer from a robber, against שמואל.

steps.title: Who does the robber collect from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא presses the ברייתא about שבח. Read plainly, it says the robber collects, which makes no sense. So it must mean a robber who sold the field to a buyer who improved it.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If it is just as the ברייתא says, who would a גזלן collect from? It must be that he stole a field, sold it to someone else, and that buyer improved it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the ברייתא from step 16 actually works. It shows that the case must involve a robber who sold the field to a buyer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read literally, the ברייתא says the robber collects money, but nobody owes a robber anything. The only sensible picture is a buyer who bought from the robber, improved the field, and then lost it to the real owner. That puts the ברייתא in a robbery setting, which is hard for שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How does it work?
If you say
A robber
And he improved it (added value to the field)

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If you say it is as it is taught,
phrases.notes: The ברייתא's wording makes it sound like the robber himself is the one collecting.

phrases.english: from whom does a robber collect?

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא לָאו: כְּגוֹן שֶׁגָּזַל שָׂדֶה מֵחֲבֵירוֹ
phrases.english: Rather, is it not a case where he robbed a field from his fellow
and sold it to another, and he improved it!
phrases.notes: The buyer is the one who improved the field, and he collects from the robber.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִילֵּימָא כִּדְקָתָנֵי, גַּזְלָן מִמַּאן גָּבֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the challenge from step 16 by working out the ברייתא's case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The split reading, which puts the שבח clause in a creditor case, and שמואל's view.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A robber has no one to collect from, so the ברייתא must mean a buyer from a robber. That is a robbery case, not a creditor case.

steps.title: If you add details, read it as a creditor
steps.stepSummary: שמואל can answer that you already had to add details to make the ברייתא work. So you may just as well read it as a בעל חוב case.
steps.simpleTranslation: He can tell you: aren't you already fixing up the ברייתא? Then fix it to be about a בעל חוב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for שמואל. Since the ברייתא needs extra details no matter what, those details can describe a creditor case instead of a robber.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenger had to add 'he sold it to someone else' to the ברייתא. Once you are adding details anyway, nothing forces the robbery picture. The case can be a buyer who loses the field to the seller's creditor, which fits שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: He can say to you (an answer on someone's behalf)
You are fixing up / reinterpreting the text
A creditor

phrases.english: He could say to you:
phrases.notes: 'He' is שמואל; the גמרא is answering for him.

phrases.english: Aren't you fixing up the text anyway?
Fix it up as a creditor case too.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָךְ: לָאו תָּרוֹצֵי קָא מְתָרְצַתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 17.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא must be about a robber who sold the field.
steps.terutzMaskana: Since the ברייתא needs added details either way, it can be read as a creditor case.

steps.title: A second ברייתא about produce
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings another ברייתא, this one explaining the produce clause. A robbed field is taken away. The principal is collected from sold property and the produce from free property.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: How does eating produce work? Someone stole a field and it is taken out of his hands. When he collects, he collects the principal from sold property and the produce from free property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא to challenge שמואל again. This one explains the produce part of the משנה using a robbed field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ברייתא has the same structure as the one about שבח, but it deals with produce. It again talks about a robbed field and someone collecting. That sets up the same question of who is really collecting, which comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Eating produce (the value of the crops)
The principal (the field's own value)
Liened property that has already been sold to others
Free property the person still owns

phrases.english: Come and hear:
For eating produce, how is it?
Here is one who robbed a field from his fellow
and it is taken out from his possession,
when he collects, he collects the principal
from liened property,
and the produce he collects from free property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the שבח ברייתא was answered, the גמרא brings a parallel ברייתא about produce.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: This ברייתא also explains the משנה's law with a robbed field, which suggests a robbery setting that is hard for שמואל.

steps.title: Again: who does the robber collect from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks the same question about the produce ברייתא. A robber has no one to collect from, so it must be a robber who sold the field to a buyer who improved it.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If it is just as taught, who would a גזלן collect from? It must be that he stole a field, sold it to someone else, and that buyer improved it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats its earlier question, this time about the produce ברייתא. It shows that this case too must be a buyer from a robber.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These are the same words as step 17, but now they are aimed at the new ברייתא. The plain wording has the robber collecting, which cannot be right. So the case is a buyer who bought from a robber, and the challenge to שמואל comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, is it not that... (pushing toward a forced reading)
And he sold it to another person

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a copying mistake. The גמרא really repeats the same question, but now it is about the produce ברייתא, not the שבח one.

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If you say it is as it is taught,
from whom does a robber collect?

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא לָאו: כְּגוֹן שֶׁגָּזַל שָׂדֶה מֵחֲבֵירוֹ
phrases.english: Rather, is it not a case where he robbed a field from his fellow
and sold it to another, and he improved it!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִילֵּימָא כִּדְקָתָנֵי, גַּזְלָן מִמַּאן גָּבֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same reasoning as step 17 on the new ברייתא from step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's view, through the produce ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A robber cannot collect from anyone, so the ברייתא must describe a buyer from a robber. That is a robbery case, which is hard for שמואל.

steps.title: רבא: The robber ate the produce and dug up the field
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains the produce ברייתא as a case where the robber himself ate the produce and damaged the field. The victim collects the principal from sold property and the produce from free property.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: What case are we dealing with here? Someone stole a field full of produce from his friend. He ate the produce and dug pits, ditches and caves in it. When the victim comes to collect the principal, he collects it from sold property. When the victim comes to collect the produce, he collects it from free property.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question from step 20. He shows that the ברייתא can be about the robber himself, with no buyer involved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question was that a plain robber has nobody to collect from, so the case seemed to need a buyer. רבא says the person collecting is the victim, and he collects from the robber. The robber ruined the field by digging, so the victim is owed its value (the principal). The robber also ate the produce, so he owes for that too. The principal can be taken even from property the robber sold, but the produce only from property he still owns.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to narrow a source to a specific case)
The robbery victim
The principal, meaning the main value of the field itself
Liened property, meaning property the debtor already sold to others
Free property, meaning property the debtor still owns
Pits, ditches and caves, which are kinds of digging that ruin a field

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the victim is collecting from a buyer here. In רבא's case the victim collects from the robber, and the sold property only matters as a place to collect the principal from.
steps.whyThisMatters: For the produce ברייתא, step 18's creditor answer cannot work, because a creditor does not collect produce (step 13). So רבא gives a case with no buyer at all: the victim collecting from the robber himself.

phrases.english: Rava said: With what are we dealing here?
For example, where he stole a field from his friend,
full of produce,
and he ate the produce,
and dug pits, ditches and caves in it.
When the victim comes to collect the principal,
phrases.notes: The principal here means the field's value before the robber damaged it.

phrases.english: he collects from liened property;
when the victim comes to collect the produce,
he collects from free property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 20 by giving a case where the robber himself is the one paying.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining the case (אוקימתא): the robber himself ate the produce and damaged the field.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A plain robber has no one to collect from, so the ברייתא must be about a buyer who improved the field.
steps.terutzMaskana: The victim collects from the robber: the principal of the ruined field from sold property, and the eaten produce from free property. No buyer is needed.

steps.title: רבה bar רב הונא begins another explanation
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא starts a different way to explain the case in the ברייתא. His words continue on the next עמוד.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא said: For example, where...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a second answer to the same question. רבה בר רב הונא begins describing his own case, and the rest of his words come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like רבא, he opens with "for example, where," which means he is also defining a specific case for the ברייתא. We have to wait for the next lines to see how his case differs from רבא's.

keyTerms.meaning: For example, where; introduces a specific case
